```markdown
# Breaking-change flag for release notes

Source: `specs/deferred_items.md`, item 7.

## Intent

`release-notes` writes one bullet per merged pull request. Some of those pull
requests break things for users. Today nothing in a bullet says so.

Two readers need to know:

- A person who reads the release notes must see breaking changes at a glance.
- `announce` must put breaking changes first in its post.

`changelog-check` parses the same output. It must accept the new marker and
keep accepting every bullet it accepts today.

## Goals

- `release-notes` marks a bullet as breaking when its pull request carries the
  `breaking` label.
- `changelog-check/parse.py` reads the marker and records it on the entry.
- `announce` lists breaking entries before all other entries.
- Bullets without the marker parse exactly as they do today.

## Non-goals

- No other flags or labels (for example `security` or `deprecation`).
- No change to the bullet text after the marker.
- No rewrite of release notes that already exist.

## Anti-goals

- Any change that makes an older, untagged bullet fail `changelog-check`.
- Any change to how `parse.py` splits on " — " for untagged bullets.

## Constraints

- `parse.py` splits each bullet on " — " and rejects a bullet with more than
  two parts. That rule stays.
- The marker must not add a third " — " part.

## Approaches

1. **Third part.** Append " — breaking: yes" to the bullet. Teach `parse.py` to
   accept three parts. This loosens the two-part rule for every bullet, and
   readers find the flag at the end of the line.
2. **Leading tag.** Start the bullet with `[breaking]`. `parse.py` strips the tag
   before it splits. Untagged bullets take the exact same path as today. Readers
   see the tag first.

**Picked: 2.** Older notes stay valid with no change, and the tag sits where a
reader looks first.

## Decided

- `release-notes` writes `[breaking] ` (tag, then one space) at the start of a
  bullet when the pull request has the `breaking` label.
- `parse.py` checks for a leading `[breaking]`. If present, it strips the tag and
  the space after it, then splits the rest on " — " under the current rules. It
  sets `breaking=True` on the entry. Otherwise it sets `breaking=False`.
- `announce` lists entries with `breaking=True` first.
- A test in `skills/changelog-check/` covers one tagged bullet and one untagged
  bullet.

## My calls (not discussed)

- The tag match is exact and case-sensitive: `[breaking]` only. A bullet that
  starts with `[Breaking]` parses as untagged.
- `announce` keeps the original order inside each group (breaking, then the
  rest). It keeps the `[breaking]` text in the post so readers of the post see
  it too.
- The test also checks that a tagged bullet with three " — " parts still fails.

## Left to the builder

- How `release-notes` reads pull request labels today, and where the label
  check goes.
- The name and location of the test file inside `skills/changelog-check/`.
```

I made 3 calls that we did not discuss. They are in the spec under "My calls":

- The tag match is exact and case-sensitive.
- `announce` keeps the original order inside each group, and keeps the `[breaking]` text in its post.
- The test also checks that a tagged bullet with three parts still fails.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The leading tag is safe because `parse.py` strips it before the " — " split. The two-part rule never sees the tag.
- An untagged bullet goes through the same code path as before. That is why older notes need no migration.
- The three-part test guards the boundary. It proves that the tag does not let a malformed bullet through.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
